heuristics.rule: Use sector-specific return viability, not generic 'career' comparisons
heuristics.condition: When evaluating whether to return to home country...
heuristics.action: ...first classify your sector into one of: Tech/AI, Finance (PE/VC vs. state), Academia, Medicine, Law/Government — because each has a different ceiling, income compression, and hiring market
heuristics.because: A framework that treats 'career' as one undifferentiated thing will give wrong answers for most people; the returnee premium, licensing friction, and competitive dynamics vary dramatically by field

heuristics.rule: Compare net savings in PPP-adjusted terms, not gross income in nominal USD
heuristics.condition: When an income compression figure feels prohibitive...
heuristics.action: ...calculate actual annual savings in each scenario rather than comparing gross salaries, adjusting for cost of living
heuristics.because: A $400K US physician saving $80K/year may do worse in wealth accumulation than a Chinese physician earning ¥600K saving ¥300K/year in PPP-adjusted terms — the compression is real but must be measured against what you actually keep

heuristics.rule: Treat license incompatibility as a hard blocker, not a soft friction
heuristics.condition: When a professional in medicine or law is considering return...
heuristics.action: ...research exact re-licensing requirements before treating return as a viable near-term option
heuristics.because: US MD and US JD credentials do not transfer directly to Chinese or Indian clinical/legal practice; the re-qualification pathway is long, difficult, and conducted in a different language/legal system — it is a structural barrier, not merely administrative overhead

heuristics.rule: In China, distinguish private-market roles from state-institution roles before assuming returnee premium applies
heuristics.condition: When evaluating finance or government opportunities in China...
heuristics.action: ...assess whether the specific role sits inside state-owned enterprises, state banks, or government — and if so, discount the returnee premium significantly
heuristics.because: Senior leadership in state-owned banks and government civil service tends to go to Party-connected domestic candidates; the returnee premium is real in PE/VC/tech but largely absent in state institutions

heuristics.rule: For academia returnees to China, evaluate the field-specific academic freedom constraint before accepting recruitment packages
heuristics.condition: When a US-trained academic in social sciences, humanities, or politically sensitive STEM is considering Chinese talent programs...
heuristics.action: ...weight academic freedom constraints heavily, not just the financial package
heuristics.because: China's recruitment packages are financially genuine, but research freedom in social sciences, humanities, and dual-use STEM fields is materially constrained — the package value is diminished if it limits research agenda

decision_factors.why_it_matters: US experience commands a strong premium in some sectors (Tech, PE/VC, Academia in China) and near-zero premium in others (state banking, government civil service) — this directly determines compensation and career trajectory upon return
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Research whether companies in your specific sector actively recruit US-experienced candidates; check if talent programs or headhunters in your field specifically target US returnees; look at leadership profiles at target employers

decision_factors.why_it_matters: For medicine and law, credentials earned in the US do not automatically qualify practice in China or India — re-licensing may require passing exams in a different language on a different legal/medical system, which is a hard structural barrier
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Identify the exact re-qualification pathway for your profession in your target country; estimate time and cost; determine whether the path is realistically completable given your current language proficiency and time since training

decision_factors.why_it_matters: The compression ranges from moderate (Tech: 30–50%) to severe (Medicine: 70–85%); this determines whether the return is financially viable and changes the entire savings/wealth-building calculus
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Benchmark current US total comp against realistic total comp at equivalent-level roles in target country; convert to PPP-adjusted terms; calculate net savings rate in each scenario rather than comparing gross figures

decision_factors.factor: Political and regulatory risk in target sector
decision_factors.why_it_matters: China's regulatory environment has become more restrictive since 2021 — finance and tech sectors have faced crackdowns; this creates career and income volatility that is not captured in a point-in-time salary comparison
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Track sector-specific regulatory history in target country over the past 3–5 years; assess whether your target sector has been subject to government restrictions; evaluate downside scenarios if regulatory crackdown hits your employer

decision_factors.factor: Career ceiling at VP/CXO level by sector and country
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Some sectors (Tech in China, PE/VC) allow returnees to reach senior leadership; others (state banks, government) structurally exclude returnees from top roles — this determines long-term career trajectory, not just entry-level compensation
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Research the leadership profiles of senior executives (VP and above) at target employer types; determine what fraction are returnees vs. domestic-track; look for patterns in who gets promoted to C-suite

decision_factors.why_it_matters: For academic returnees, the quality of lab infrastructure, funding availability, and institutional reputation determines whether they can maintain international research competitiveness — a weak institution can stall a research career regardless of the recruitment package
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Evaluate Nature/Science publication rates at target institution; assess startup fund adequacy for your specific research area; check whether returnees at that institution have maintained international collaboration and publication rates post-return

decision_factors.factor: Private vs. state sector distinction within country
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Within the same country, private-sector and state-sector roles have fundamentally different dynamics for returnees — the returnee premium, promotion ceiling, and regulatory exposure differ dramatically
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Classify each specific opportunity as private-market, state-owned enterprise, or government; apply the appropriate ceiling and premium assessment for each category rather than treating the country as uniform

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Returning to clinical medicine in China
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: The US MD credential does not permit clinical practice without passing Chinese licensing exams conducted in Mandarin on Chinese medical systems — the return is not to clinical medicine but to a multi-year re-qualification process or to research/teaching/admin roles with significantly lower income
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: US-trained physicians who assume their credential travels and plan to continue practicing clinically

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Accepting a Chinese state-owned bank or government-adjacent finance role as a returnee
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Senior leadership positions in these institutions tend to go to Party-connected domestic candidates; the returnee premium that exists in PE/VC does not apply here, and career ceiling is reached earlier and more definitively
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Finance professionals who treat all China finance opportunities as equivalent without distinguishing state vs. private sector

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Taking a Chinese academic talent program recruitment package
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: In social sciences, humanities, and politically sensitive STEM fields, the research agenda is materially constrained by academic freedom limitations — the financial package is genuine, but what you can actually research may be narrowed significantly post-arrival
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Social scientists, humanists, and dual-use STEM researchers who evaluate the offer primarily on financial terms

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Staying in the US as a physician to preserve high income
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: A $400K US physician saving $80K/year may accumulate less real wealth than a Chinese physician earning ¥600K saving ¥300K/year in PPP-adjusted terms — the gross income advantage does not translate proportionally into savings advantage
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: High-earning US professionals in high-cost-of-living areas who compare gross salaries without accounting for savings rate and cost of living differentials

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Returning to India for services-sector tech roles (TCS, Infosys)
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: These roles are structurally less attractive for returning FAANG engineers — the credential and skill level is mismatched, and the career trajectory and compensation are not commensurate with US experience; the Indian tech return premium exists primarily at unicorns and FAANG India offices, not at services firms
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: India-origin tech professionals who treat all Indian tech employers as equivalent without distinguishing FAANG India/unicorns from IT services

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Pursuing a law or government policy role upon return
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: A US JD does not qualify practice of Chinese or Indian law; government civil service tracks are domestic-entry; the best available path — compliance or GC at MNC — is a significant scope reduction from senior legal practice, and think tank roles are competitive with limited slots
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: US-trained lawyers and policy professionals who assume their credentials and experience translate into comparable roles in their home country

failure_patterns.pattern: Treating income compression as a fixed number rather than a net savings comparison
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: People anchor on gross salary figures in USD, which makes home country income look drastically worse; the cognitive default is to compare the largest visible number without adjusting for taxes, cost of living, and actual savings rate
failure_patterns.consequence: Professionals reject financially rational return decisions because they are comparing the wrong metric — they overestimate the US income advantage and underestimate the home country wealth-building potential
warning_signs: Saying 'I'd be taking a 60% pay cut' without having calculated net savings in both scenarios
Comparing gross salary in USD without PPP adjustment or cost-of-living normalization

failure_patterns.pattern: Assuming sector-level optimism applies to a specific sub-sector or employer type
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Positive signals about 'China tech' or 'India finance' get generalized to all employers in those geographies; people read about ByteDance salaries and apply them to state-owned tech companies, or read about Sequoia India and assume it applies to domestic banking
failure_patterns.consequence: Professionals accept roles expecting returnee premium and growth trajectories that do not exist in their specific employer category, leading to early career ceiling and compensation disappointment
warning_signs: Evaluating a state-owned enterprise role using PE/VC compensation benchmarks
Not explicitly classifying a target employer as private-market vs. state-sector before accepting an offer

failure_patterns.pattern: Underestimating license re-qualification as a short-term administrative step
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Professionals in medicine and law assume that strong credentials and experience will expedite or partially substitute for formal re-licensing; the difficulty of passing licensing exams in a different language and legal/medical system is underestimated
failure_patterns.consequence: Professionals return expecting to practice their profession and find themselves blocked from clinical or legal practice for years, forced into research, teaching, or administrative roles that are lower-income and off their intended career path
warning_signs: Saying 'I'll figure out the licensing once I'm back' without a concrete plan
Not having researched the specific exam requirements, language of examination, or pass rates for returnees in their field

failure_patterns.pattern: Ignoring regulatory and political risk in sector selection
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Return decisions are made based on current conditions and current salary benchmarks; the 2020–2021 regulatory crackdowns in China (Ant Financial, private tutoring, gaming) were not predicted by people who had made return decisions in 2018–2019 based on then-attractive conditions
failure_patterns.consequence: Professionals build careers in sectors that face sudden regulatory restriction, leading to layoffs, income loss, or forced sector pivots that would have been avoidable with greater attention to policy risk signals
warning_signs: Evaluating a China finance or edtech opportunity without researching the sector's regulatory history since 2020
Treating current salary benchmarks as stable without assessing sector-specific political exposure

diagnostic_questions.question: Is your profession subject to country-specific licensing requirements?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the return is to the same professional role or to a fundamentally different one — medicine and law face hard barriers; tech and finance do not
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: What is the exact re-qualification pathway, how long does it take, is the exam conducted in your home language, and what is the pass rate for returnees?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Does your US credential and experience carry a genuine premium in your target sector, or is it neutral to slightly positive?

diagnostic_questions.question: Is your target employer private-market or state-owned / government-affiliated?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the returnee premium and career ceiling assumptions that apply to private-sector roles also apply to your specific opportunity — they often do not in state institutions
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Has the state institution historically promoted returnees to senior leadership, or does that tier tend to go to domestic-track candidates?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Is the private employer in a sector that has faced or is at risk of regulatory restriction in your target country?

diagnostic_questions.question: What is your actual net savings rate in the US versus what it would be in your home country at the target role?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the income compression is as severe as the gross salary comparison suggests, or whether cost of living and tax differences close the gap significantly
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If net savings are comparable or higher at home, what non-financial factors are driving the preference to stay in the US?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Is the net savings gap large enough to be a definitive factor, or is it within the range that personal and family considerations could reasonably override?

diagnostic_questions.question: Which specific sector are you in — Tech/AI, Finance (PE/VC vs. state), Academia, Medicine, Law/Government, or Entrepreneurship?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: The baseline return viability, income compression range, and career ceiling risk — these differ so significantly across sectors that the sector answer largely determines the initial prior on return viability
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Within that sector, are you targeting the sub-segment with strong returnee demand (e.g., AI research, PE/VC) or the weaker sub-segment (e.g., state banking, IT services)?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Not applicable — sector classification is a required input, not a yes/no question

diagnostic_questions.question: For China-return candidates in academia: what is your research field?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether academic freedom constraints materially limit your research agenda — STEM in non-sensitive areas faces fewer constraints than social sciences, humanities, or politically sensitive STEM
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If you are in a constrained field, have you assessed whether you can maintain your current research agenda at the target institution, or would it require meaningful redirection?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If you are in a field without significant academic freedom constraints, the Chinese talent program packages represent strong financial and career value relative to US alternatives

diagnostic_questions.question: Are you benchmarking against the right peer set at target Indian or Chinese employers?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the salary and career trajectory data being used reflects comparable roles — FAANG India/unicorn compensation is not representative of IT services, and PE/VC China compensation is not representative of state banks
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Have you verified compensation and career ceiling data specifically for returnees at that employer tier, not just the sector broadly?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: The decision may be based on unrepresentative benchmarks that will produce surprises post-joining

industry_realities.common_belief: A US MD or JD credential travels internationally and allows you to continue practicing in your home country
industry_realities.actual_reality: Medical and legal licenses are country-specific; a US MD must pass Chinese medical licensing exams in Mandarin to practice clinically in China; a US JD must pass a separate bar qualification to practice Indian or Chinese law — the credential does not transfer
industry_realities.implication: Medical and legal professionals must treat return as a career transition, not a credential transfer — and plan for a multi-year re-qualification process or a pivot to research, teaching, compliance, or entrepreneurship roles

industry_realities.common_belief: China's talent recruitment programs (Thousand Talents, Yangtze River Scholar) are primarily bureaucratic or symbolic
industry_realities.actual_reality: The packages are financially substantive — research startup funds of ¥500K–¥5M, salary supplements, housing subsidies, and lab setup funding are real and actively deployed; Chinese scientific output is now internationally competitive in STEM fields
industry_realities.implication: Academic returnees to China should evaluate these programs seriously as financial and career propositions, not dismiss them — the main constraint is field-specific academic freedom, not program credibility

industry_realities.common_belief: Income compression means the return is financially inferior
industry_realities.actual_reality: Gross income compression (30–85% depending on sector) does not translate proportionally into savings or wealth compression; a physician earning 70% less in China may save 3–4x more annually in PPP-adjusted terms because cost of living differentials are large
industry_realities.implication: Evaluate return economics on net savings rate and PPP-adjusted wealth accumulation, not gross salary comparison — the decision calculus changes significantly when the right metric is used

industry_realities.common_belief: 'China tech' or 'India finance' return opportunity is broadly positive, so a specific role in that sector should be attractive
industry_realities.actual_reality: Within each country and sector, there is a dramatic split between private-market roles (where returnee premium is real) and state-owned or government-affiliated roles (where career ceiling is real and returnee premium is weak) — the sector-level signal does not apply uniformly
industry_realities.implication: Evaluate each specific employer and role type rather than using country-sector aggregate signals; the state/private distinction is the most important sub-classification within any sector

industry_realities.common_belief: Returning to India for tech means going to TCS, Infosys, or Wipro
industry_realities.actual_reality: IT services firms are explicitly identified as less attractive for returning FAANG engineers; the relevant return market is FAANG India offices, Indian unicorns (Flipkart, Swiggy, Zepto), and AI/ML research roles — which have materially different compensation and career trajectories
industry_realities.implication: India-origin tech professionals should specifically target the unicorn and MNC India office tier, not the IT services tier — the returnee premium does not exist at IT services for someone with senior US tech experience

industry_realities.common_belief: China's regulatory crackdowns on tech and finance were one-time events and the sector has stabilized
industry_realities.actual_reality: The source identifies finance sector regulatory scrutiny as an ongoing and increased risk since 2021; the Ant Financial IPO cancellation, private tutoring restrictions, and gaming limits represent a pattern of government intervention in private-sector activity
industry_realities.implication: China finance and consumer tech return decisions should include explicit scenario planning for regulatory risk, not just point-in-time compensation benchmarking

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: How they compare income across geographies
junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Compares gross salary in USD — sees '60% compression' and treats the decision as financially irrational
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Calculates net savings rate in each scenario, adjusts for PPP and cost of living, and evaluates wealth accumulation trajectory rather than gross income
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: The gross comparison leads to rejecting financially sound decisions; the net savings comparison reveals that compression is often much less severe than it appears and occasionally reverses

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: How they evaluate a sector-level return signal
junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Reads that 'China tech' or 'India finance' is strong for returnees and applies that signal to their specific opportunity without further decomposition
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Immediately sub-classifies the specific employer as private-market vs. state-sector, identifies which sub-segment of the sector they are targeting, and applies the appropriate ceiling and premium assessment for that sub-segment
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Aggregate sector signals mask dramatic within-sector variation; applying a PE/VC premium assumption to a state bank role leads to misaligned expectations and early career ceiling surprises

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Assumes a strong US credential (MD, JD) will be recognized and valued in the home country, treating re-qualification as a minor administrative step
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Identifies upfront whether the profession requires country-specific licensing, researches the exact re-qualification pathway, and classifies the return as a continuation vs. a career transition accordingly
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Treating a hard licensing barrier as administrative overhead leads to returns that strand professionals outside their intended practice area for years

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: How they assess long-term career ceiling
junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Evaluates entry-level and mid-level compensation and assumes the upward trajectory is comparable to the US
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Researches the leadership profiles at VP and C-suite level at target employer types to determine whether returnees reach senior roles or hit a structural ceiling driven by domestic-track preferences or political considerations
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Entry and mid-level opportunities may be strong even where the long-term ceiling is real; a 10-year career decision based only on entry conditions will produce different outcomes than one that models the ceiling

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: How they factor regulatory and political risk
junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Makes a return decision based on current conditions and current salary benchmarks without modeling downside scenarios
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Reviews the sector's regulatory history over 3–5 years in the target country, identifies whether the sector has been subject to government intervention, and builds downside scenarios into the decision
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Point-in-time conditions can reverse rapidly in regulated sectors; the 2018–2019 China finance returnee who did not model regulatory risk faced the 2021 crackdowns without preparation
